latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Varicella-zoster virus reactivates from sensory or cranial nerve ganglia, or less often follows primary varicella with hematogenous or neural CNS spread. This mechanism covers the entry state for VZV encephalitis, not isolated zoster skin disease.

VZV DNA and antigen burden in CSF-adjacent, meningeal, ependymal, vascular, glial, or neuronal compartments sustains positive CSF PCR or intrathecal antibody response and drives antiviral-responsive disease activity.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Ganglion, radicular, cranial nerve, and dermatomal spread
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: VZV tropism for sensory ganglia and cranial nerves produces dermatomal vesicular rash when skin is involved, and can also produce zoster sine herpete, cranial neuropathy, radiculitis, myelitis, or meningoradicular imaging without a visible rash.
Viral antigen, blood-CSF barrier injury, and meningeal immune activation produce headache, meningismus, CSF pleocytosis, high CSF protein, and often normal or mildly reduced CSF glucose.

Inflammation in cortical, subcortical, cerebellar, brainstem, ependymal, or multifocal brain tissue produces encephalopathy, psychiatric or behavioral change, seizures, focal deficits, and non-HSV-pattern MRI abnormalities.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: VZV small- and large-vessel CNS vasculopathy
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: VZV can infect or inflame cerebral arteries and perivascular spaces, causing multifocal stenosis, vessel enhancement, ischemic infarction, hemorrhage, or stroke-like deficits. Vasculopathy can coexist with encephalitis and may occur with or without rash.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Cortical irritation and seizure network activation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Cortical inflammation, hemorrhagic lesions, ischemia, edema, or metabolic stress in VZV encephalitis lowers seizure threshold and can lead to focal seizures, generalized seizures, or status epilepticus.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Cerebral edema, coma, and intracranial pressure pathway
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Inflammatory lesions, vasculopathy, hemorrhage, and blood-brain barrier injury can produce edema, depressed consciousness, raised intracranial pressure, herniation, and ICU-level mortality risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Delayed or inadequate active antiviral exposure
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Ongoing VZV replication and vascular inflammation before adequate active antiviral exposure raises accumulated neurologic injury, vasculopathy, disability, and mortality. This mechanism is modulated by renal dosing, absorption, resistance, and treatment timing.

The same reactivation process can manifest in dermatomes, cranial nerves, roots, or zoster sine herpete.

Measured fever is common but variable.
Meningeal inflammation and pressure physiology produce headache.
Meningitis, raised pressure, or brainstem involvement can produce nausea and vomiting.
Meningeal irritation can produce photophobia.
VZV encephalitis often has meningoencephalitis CSF and exam features.

axes.clinical_baseline_context: Usually normal in isolated encephalitis; can fall with aspiration, respiratory failure, coma, or critical illness.
Rash absence does not exclude VZV CNS disease.
Persistent encephalopathy separates VZV encephalitis from uncomplicated VZV meningitis.

Dermatomal vesicles are a specific phenotype within the rash parent finding.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Acyclovir-resistant VZV requires alternative active coverage.
Renal failure requires dose adjustment and close toxicity monitoring without abandoning active CNS therapy.
Poor hydration raises crystal nephropathy risk and can force interruption.

side_effects.interpretation: Crystal nephropathy risk rises with renal impairment, dehydration, or rapid infusion.
Acyclovir can worsen kidney injury in susceptible patients.

treatments.context_specific_role: Definitive antiviral vector for VZV CNS replication while diagnostics, renal dosing, and complication management proceed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Vomiting, malabsorption, or unreliable oral intake reduces exposure.
Renal dosing and neurotoxicity monitoring are required.

side_effects.interpretation: Renal toxicity is less common than IV acyclovir but still relevant.

treatments.context_specific_role: Stepdown after stabilization or extended coverage when IV therapy has controlled acute CNS replication.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Foscarnet does not require viral thymidine kinase activation.
Foscarnet nephrotoxicity and electrolyte toxicity can constrain exposure.

side_effects.interpretation: Foscarnet renal toxicity can be clinically limiting.

treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative active antiviral vector when acyclovir cannot provide adequate activity.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Steroids without active antiviral coverage risk permitting viral replication.
Profound immunosuppression raises opportunistic infection risk.

side_effects.interpretation: Immunosuppression can worsen effective control if antiviral exposure is inadequate.

treatments.context_specific_role: Inflammation- and vasculopathy-modulating vector, not a standalone antiviral.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Antiseizure therapy treats seizure physiology rather than VZV replication.

treatments.context_specific_role: Controls seizure-driven injury while antiviral therapy reshapes VZV replication.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: ICP-directed therapy only helps pressure physiology.

side_effects.interpretation: Sedation can worsen apparent mental status.

treatments.context_specific_role: Temporizes coma, airway risk, oxygenation, and pressure physiology while antiviral treatment works.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Renal protection value is larger when baseline renal reserve is poor.

treatments.context_specific_role: Preserves feasible active antiviral exposure by reducing renal toxicity and dosing errors.

present.trajectory_modulation: Older adults have higher zoster reactivation risk, more vasculopathy, more severe encephalopathy, and worse recovery reserve.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Lower cognitive reserve can make encephalopathy more apparent.

severe_cellular_immunosuppression_contex.trajectory_modulation: Raises reactivation, dissemination, high viral burden, acyclovir resistance concern, and severe CNS complications; fever and CSF pleocytosis may be blunted.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Profound immunosuppression can reduce cellular CSF response despite severe disease.
Higher viral burden increases PCR detectability.
Immunosuppressed hosts have higher severe disease risk.
Resistance is concentrated in immunocompromised hosts after antiviral selection pressure.

zoster_sine_herpete_or_missed_rash.trajectory_modulation: Does not lower the biological possibility of VZV CNS disease enough to exclude it; it mainly shifts diagnostic reliance toward CSF VZV PCR, intrathecal antibody, MRI, and neurologic syndrome.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: No visible vesicular rash is compatible with VZV CNS disease.
Absent rash with VZV-positive CSF raises zoster sine herpete context.

present.trajectory_modulation: A recent dermatomal vesicular eruption strongly increases the VZV CNS disease prior when encephalopathy, seizures, focal deficits, or CSF inflammation occur.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Dermatomal vesicles are a specific reactivation clue.

present.trajectory_modulation: Does not cause VZV but allows viral replication, vasculopathy, edema, and irreversible CNS injury to accumulate.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Delayed active antiviral exposure raises residual deficit risk.

present.trajectory_modulation: Renal dysfunction does not define VZV encephalitis but changes antiviral exposure, toxicity, and interruption risk.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Acyclovir nephrotoxicity rises with renal impairment and dehydration.
Renal dosing errors can underdose or interrupt therapy.

present.trajectory_modulation: Baseline vascular disease does not prove VZV, but VZV vasculopathy superimposed on low reserve raises stroke and hemorrhage severity.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Vasculopathy makes focal deficit more likely.

supportive_care: Treat suspected VZV encephalitis as time-sensitive CNS infection: encephalopathy, seizure, focal deficit, or brain parenchymal MRI abnormalities with zoster context or CSF inflammation should not wait for late confirmatory testing before active antiviral coverage.

Separate VZV encephalitis from isolated VZV meningitis: persistent altered mental status, psychiatric or behavioral change, seizures, focal deficits, cranial neuropathy, stroke-like events, or brain parenchymal/vascular MRI lesions should drive the encephalitis manifold.

Lumbar puncture when safe: record opening pressure, CSF WBC and differential, RBC count, protein, glucose with paired serum glucose, bacterial studies, HSV and VZV PCR, and intrathecal VZV antibody when PCR is negative or delayed.
Brain MRI with DWI/ADC, FLAIR, T2, GRE/SWI, contrast, and vascular imaging when focal deficits, hemorrhage, infarct pattern, or vasculopathy are suspected; CT can be normal or nonspecific early.
Do not use rash absence to exclude VZV CNS disease; zoster sine herpete and missed or atypical rash are clinically real.
Track neurologic exam serially: orientation, attention, behavior, hallucinations, language, cranial nerves, motor asymmetry, gait, seizure recurrence, and Glasgow Coma Scale when severe.
Use EEG for unexplained fluctuating consciousness, seizures, or concern for nonconvulsive status epilepticus.

Monitor acyclovir safety and exposure: baseline and daily creatinine during IV therapy, adequate hydration, renal dose adjustment, avoidance of unnecessary nephrotoxins, and reassessment if renal dysfunction forces underdosing.

For suspected VZV vasculopathy, document vascular imaging, infarct or hemorrhage pattern, stroke deficits, and active antiviral exposure; steroids, when used, are adjunctive and should not replace antiviral therapy.
Provide ICU-level support for coma, status epilepticus, raised ICP, respiratory compromise, hemodynamic instability, or rapidly progressive focal deficits.
Plan rehabilitation and follow-up for survivors: cognition, psychiatric symptoms, cranial neuropathy, hearing, gait, myelopathy, seizure risk, and delayed vasculopathy relapse.
distillation_quality_notes: Disease-specific medical input is only Varicella-zoster virus encephalitis; rash, immunosuppression, vasculopathy, stroke, meningitis-only presentations, and treatment context are represented as axes, mechanisms, risk factors, and modifiers.
CSF VZV PCR and intrathecal VZV antibody are modeled as measurable axes because pathogen identity is not reliably emergent from routine vitals, symptoms, CSF cell counts, or MRI alone.
